Issued at 530 AM CDT Sun Sep 6 2026

An omega pattern is in place across North America early this 
morning, with deep upper lows spinning over the Pacific 
Northwest and Canadian maritime provinces and a ridge axis over
the US Plains. The local area is just upstream of the ridge 
axis, and the resulting southwest flow aloft with broad 
isentropic ascent and underlying warm air advection has 
initiated scattered showers and isolated thunderstorms across 
southwest and south central North Dakota. At the surface, low 
pressure is analyzed over the Black Hills with an inverted 
trough extending north along the MT/ND border. A broad easterly
surface flow over much of the state has led to patchy dense fog
and very low stratus against the sloping terrain along the 
Highway 52 corridor from northern parts of the state to the 
James River Valley.

As has been the case the past few days, the convective forecast
through this evening is highly uncertain. Each run of each CAM 
seemingly offers a solution different from all others, and none 
of them have properly simulated what is being observed early 
this morning. Broad synoptic scale lift is forecast to be 
present over western and central North Dakota throughout the 
day. But if, where, and when storms develop and/or intensify 
will likely be determined by the evolution of mesoscale 
features that carry low predictability beyond a forecast time 
range of a few hours. Mixed layer capping also contributes 
uncertainty to the convective forecast this afternoon, with low 
level wind trajectories mostly unfavorable for strong boundary 
layer mixing. One potential feature to keep an eye on that 
recent deterministic and high-resolution ensemble guidance has 
consolidated on is a west-to-east oriented surface warm front 
that is forecast to sharpen across central North Dakota this 
afternoon. Ignoring convective inhibition for surface and mixed-
layer based parcels, the forecast environment is favorable for 
severe storms with CAPE on the order of 2500-3500 J/kg and deep 
layer shear ranging from around 30 kts south to near 50 kts 
north. Storm mode may be mixed, but any convection initiating 
along the warm front could quickly become linear with a 
damaging wind threat given shear and deep layer wind vectors 
being parallel to the front. Regardless of mode, any storm or 
complex thereof along the warm front could be in a favorable 
environment for tornadogenesis, although modeled hodographs 
tend to favor crosswise vorticity over streamwise. 

From this evening into tonight, the low level jet will 
reintensify over the western Dakotas ahead of much stronger 
shortwave energy ejecting from the base of the upstream 
longwave trough. This could initiate another round of strong to
severe storms, but any effects from daytime convection could 
alter this potential. By Labor Day morning, strong DCVA and lee
cyclogenesis are forecast to reach the Northern High Plains, 
which is expected to yield widespread showers and embedded 
thunderstorms over western North Dakota, with east/northeastward
propagation through the afternoon. There is uncertainty in 
potential severe hazards and magnitudes thereof on Labor Day. 
First, the morning convection is likely to remain elevated and 
could modify the mesoscale environment for the rest of the day. 
Then in the afternoon, the phasing of forcing mechanisms 
becomes highly uncertain. The most likely outcome appears to be
a forward-propagating mid level shortwave moving through 
central North Dakota during the afternoon, leaving behind the 
lee cyclogenesis that some guidance shows could evolve into a 
double-barrel surface low from southern Saskatchewan to 
northwest South Dakota. CAMs generally indicate at least low 
probabilities for storms associated with both of these features
in the afternoon, but the arrival of a dry slot could mitigate 
convective coverage (although latest guidance appears to have 
slowed the progression and/or dampened the influence of the dry
slot). If the mid level shortwave stays ahead of the lee 
cyclone, any convection that initiates from it could be in a 
volatile environment with strong shear at all layers keeping 
all severe hazards in play, including tornadoes. But in turn, 
there could be enough residual capping to lower the threat 
ceiling. Farther west, any storms that initiate near the lee 
cyclone would more likely be high-based with a predominant 
damaging wind threat. Another aspect of the system as whole 
that will need to be monitored is the potential for excessive 
rainfall. Of note, 00Z HREF members show potential for local 
rain amounts as high as 2-3 inches across already rain-soaked 
northern parts of the state.

Forecast temperatures today through Labor Day remain above 
normal north (upper 70s to mid 80s) to well above normal south
